profile.reading:
This Lumen colocation facility, internally identified in public records as Minneapolis 3, is located at 715 North 2nd Street, Minneapolis, MN 55401; Lumen does not publish individual building addresses or specs on its own site for any of its 175-plus North American colocation sites. Lumen Technologies, formerly CenturyLink (renamed Lumen on September 14, 2020, with its stock ticker changing from CTL to LUMN on September 18, 2020) and built in part on CenturyLink's November 1, 2017 acquisition of Level 3 Communications, operates this facility as part of a network-centric edge colocation product rather than a wholesale hyperscale campus. Lumen's own colocation data sheet states more than 175 carrier-neutral data centers across more than 60 North American markets, offering cabinet power in the 3 to 15 kilowatt range described as varying by site; unlike the wholesale operators tracked elsewhere in this registry, Lumen does not disclose per-building square footage or total MW capacity for any of its sites.

Xcel Energy, Minnesota's dominant utility, has acknowledged that data center growth is pushing it to extend natural gas plant operations into the 2030s despite the state's clean-energy commitments; Minnesota division president Ryan Long said the utility may extend gas contracts to get through a portion of the 2030s, even as Xcel committed $45 billion in infrastructure investment over five years. Minnesota's 2023 clean-electricity law mandates 100% carbon-free power delivery by 2040, a target a state deputy commerce commissioner has said may be difficult to meet given the pace of data center demand. Minneapolis's city council separately approved a six-month moratorium on new data center permits, with downtown facilities exempted, reflecting rising local scrutiny of the sector's power and land-use footprint even as some officials weigh downtown data centers, like this Lumen building, as a tax-base tool rather than a target for restriction.

reading.body:
Lumen Minneapolis 3 sits in downtown Minneapolis as a carrier-neutral colocation facility within Lumen's network of 175-plus North American edge data centers. Lumen does not publish individual facility capacity, square footage, or power figures for any of its sites, disclosing only an aggregate cabinet power range of 3 to 15 kilowatts per cabinet that varies by location. This campus therefore cannot be ranked by absolute capacity, though 13 mapped facilities exist in Minnesota and only 2 publish power figures totaling 10 MW statewide.

The facility's business model targets mid-range colocation customers rather than hyperscale AI training operators, offering cabinet-density power unsuitable for the dense accelerator deployments now driving data center demand. At the published 3 to 15 kilowatt range per cabinet, even a fully utilized building would deliver far lower compute density than wholesale campuses designed for 40 kilowatts per rack or higher IT loads. Lumen's lack of published specifications means this facility cannot be assessed for relevance to AI scaling.

Minnesota's grid operator has signaled that data center growth is forcing extensions of natural gas plant operations into the 2030s despite state clean-energy targets, and Minneapolis city council imposed a six-month moratorium on new data center permits outside downtown. The state's 2040 carbon-free power mandate may be difficult to achieve given data center demand growth, creating tension between clean-energy law and the sector's expansion. Lumen's downtown colocation model may attract customers seeking tax-base benefits and legacy telecommunications infrastructure, but published capacity figures are absent from the operator's specification record.
